subject: biology
title: Homeostasis Foundations
welcome_lead: Today you'll see how your body keeps everything just right — even when the world outside changes.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology Homeostasis & Response walkthrough — nervous system, reflex arc, control of internal conditions.
final_note: You learned what homeostasis is, how the nervous system sends signals, and what a reflex arc is.

concepts.def: Keeping internal conditions stable despite outside changes
Cell that detects a stimulus like light or heat
Muscle or gland that carries out the response
Nerve cell that sends fast electrical signals
Tiny gap between neurones bridged by chemicals
Fast automatic pathway that skips the brain

walkthroughs.body_html:
Homeostasis is your body's balancing act.

Body temperature, blood glucose and water content all need to stay in a narrow safe range.

If they drift too far, enzymes stop working and cells get damaged.

The pathway is: stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.

The coordinator is your CNS — the brain or spinal cord.

Receptors detect change. Effectors (muscles or glands) do something about it.

Some responses skip the brain — they go via the spinal cord only.

The path is: sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone.

That makes them fast and automatic — protecting you before you even feel pain.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT something the body regulates by homeostasis?
options: Body temperature
Blood glucose
Eye colour
Water content

mcqs.q: In a reflex arc, what sits between a sensory neurone and a motor neurone?
options: Brain
Relay neurone
Blood vessel
Hormone

mcqs.q: What does negative feedback do in homeostasis?
options: Negative feedback makes a process get worse or amplifies the change.
Negative feedback stops the body from responding to any internal change.
It reverses a change in a controlled variable, bringing it back towards the set point.
Sweating removes excess heat by carrying it out as liquid waste.

mcqs.q: Why is a reflex action faster than a conscious response?
options: The signal does not need to be processed by the brain — it travels through a simpler reflex arc via the spinal cord.
Reflexes are faster because they use specially fast neurones not used elsewhere.
The brain decides reflexes faster than other actions because it skips thinking.
Sweating removes excess heat by carrying it out as liquid waste.

mcqs.q: How does sweating help cool you down?
options: Evaporation of sweat absorbs energy (latent heat) from the skin, lowering body temperature.
Sweat is cold and directly cools the skin on contact.
Sweating removes excess heat by carrying it out as liquid waste.
Reflexes are faster because they use specially fast neurones not used elsewhere.

mcqs.q: A reflex arc uses 3 neurones (sensory, relay, motor). How many synapses does the signal cross?
When you get cold, you start to shiver. How does shivering help raise body temperature?
options: Muscle contractions release heat through respiration.
It cools the blood to trigger warming later.
It widens skin blood vessels to gain heat.
It increases sweating to trap heat.

mcqs.q: After eating a sugary meal, the pancreas releases insulin. What is the effect on blood glucose?
options: It falls back towards normal as cells take up glucose.
It rises further to give energy.
It stays exactly the same.
It is converted into protein in the blood.

mcqs.q: Homeostasis depends on negative feedback. This means that a change in a condition triggers responses that:
options: Reverse the change, restoring the normal level
Make the change larger
Stop the body responding at all
Permanently raise the set point

mcqs.q: In a reflex arc with three neurones, where is the decision to respond effectively made?
options: In the spinal cord via the relay neurone, bypassing conscious thought
In the conscious part of the brain
In the effector muscle
In the receptor itself
